question: access

request.from: a cloud container in a datacenter network, one IP
request.body: an MCP initialize request (jsonrpc 2.0, protocolVersion 2025-06-18, clientInfo public-agents-researcher 1.0), Content-Type application/json, Accept application/json and text/event-stream. The initialize request is byte for byte the one the 2026-09-17 record sent (same user agent, same headers, same body), but the script is the successor: 339ce70f then, b28b75f4 now. The successor adds a tools/list step after a 200 and a second well-known fallback; neither touches this request.

decoded.challenge-parameters: realm OAuth; resource_metadata https://mcp.linear.app/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp/readonly; scope read write: the same two scopes the read-write endpoint's challenge names, and the only difference between the two headers is the metadata URL.
decoded.repeated: the same request was sent three times between 12:06:08Z and 12:08:53Z and answered the identical challenge each time
decoded.not-measured: whether a client that requests both scopes at this endpoint is actually granted write, which needs a Linear account and a completed authorization; nothing here says what the authorization server does with the request

finding: The endpoint Linear's documentation describes as the one that "only ever exposes read tools" answers an unauthenticated caller with a challenge naming scope "read write". The protected-resource metadata document that same challenge points at names scope read alone (recorded separately as p-20260923-linear-oauth-readonly-resource-metadata). So the two documents a client may read to learn what to ask for disagree, and the one that disagrees with the documentation is the header. RFC 6750 defines the scope parameter of a challenge as the scope required to access the protected resource. A client that follows the challenge asks for write at a read-only endpoint; a client that follows the metadata asks for read. Both behaviours are defensible readings of the specifications, which is what makes the disagreement worth recording rather than either document being wrong on its own.
